about: A way across country, told as it goes, a sentence or two and no more: setting out (by the hour and the sky), the land the road runs through (by what its cells are: water crossed, fen, wood, open fields, moor, a pass), the light going on the way, and coming in sight of where it ends (by the size of the settlement). {from} and {to} are where the way begins and ends.

lines.text: You leave {from} with the sun low behind you and the dew still on the grass.
You set out from {from} early, with your shadow long in front of you on the road.
You leave {from} in a white fog that turns the hedges to ghosts at ten paces.
You leave {from} with your hood up and the rain in your face.
It rains on and off the whole way, the soft rain that gets in everywhere.
It is cold enough to see your breath, and the ruts are hard with frost.
You walk fast to keep warm, and it does not help much.
A wind comes across the open country and leans on you the whole way.
Fog lies on the road, and things come out of it one at a time: a gate, a tree, a stone.
You set out from {from} in the full of the afternoon, the road pale with dust.
You leave {from} late, with the light already going yellow.
You go out of {from} into the dark, by what light there is.
You set out from {from}.
Partway, the road goes down to the water and through it, and up the far bank with your boots full.
The road follows the river a while, close enough to hear it, and crosses where it runs wide and shallow.
For a while the road runs along a shore, and birds get up off the water as you pass.
The road goes out across the fen on a raised bank, reed on either hand taller than a man, open water glinting through it.
Out on the fen the sky is enormous, and the only things standing up in all that flatness are you and a heron.
For an hour the road runs under trees, and the light comes down green and broken through the leaves.
The road goes into the wood, and the wood closes over it, and for a long time there is nothing to see but the next bend.
The road runs between hedges and small fields, past a farm or two where dogs bark at you over the gate.
It is easy going through open country: a mill, a ford, a man ploughing who stops to watch you go by.
The road climbs onto open moor, and the country falls away behind you in long brown folds.
Up on the tops there is nothing but heather, sky and wind, and a cairn now and then to say you are still on the road.
The road climbs into the hills, switching back and forth on itself, until the land you came from is small below you.
The light goes before you are halfway, and you walk the rest by guess and by the pale line of the road.
Night comes on while you are still on the road. An owl keeps pace with you for a while, and then thinks better of it.
{to} shows ahead a long while before you reach it: smoke, a roofline, the noise of it on the wind.
The smoke of {to} comes up over the next rise, and then the roofs.
{to} is a handful of roofs at the end of the road, and a dog that comes out to see who you are.
It is a long walk, and your feet know it by the end.
By the end of it you are hungry, footsore, and glad of the sight of anywhere at all.
